findings.title: T2 vet3lim ideation p threshold
findings.description: The p recovered from the paper's own printed interval is about .0024, roughly 2.4 times the '<.001' bound the table prints. This is the ONLY such row: the ten other '<.001' cells in Table 2 recover p-values from 1.3e-04 down to below machine epsilon, so the discrepancy is isolated rather than a systematic convention. Two innocent explanations deserve weight. First, the paper used SAS PROC SURVEY procedures, whose design-based Wald test uses finite denominator degrees of freedom; that correction makes p LARGER, not smaller, so it cannot rescue the '<.001'. Second, and more likely, it is a typesetting slip: eTable 3 prints the analogous multiple-imputation row (AOR 2.25, 1.39-3.67) as p = 0.00

findings.title: T2 multiplicity moderation family (Table 2, the 12 veteran-vs-nonveteran contrast rows)
findings.description: This is deterministic arithmetic about what the reported p-values imply, not an accusation: uncorrected testing is the norm in survey epidemiology, and the paper states its convention openly rather than concealing it. But the interval of survivors is unusually stark -- none of the three uncorrected-significant contrasts (p = .006, .03, .02) clears any of the four corrections, because the smallest is .006 against a Bonferroni threshold of .0042. These 12 contrasts are one family on the strictest reading: they come from a single fitted model, on a single sample, and jointly answer the one moderation question the paper is built around. A reader who prefers to treat the three outcome types as se

But the interval of survivors is unusually stark -- none of the three uncorrected-significant contrasts (p = .006, .03, .02) clears any of the four corrections, because the smallest is .006 against a Bonferroni threshold of .0042. These 12 contrasts are one family on the strictest reading: they come from a single fitted model, on a single sample, and jointly answer the one moderation question the paper is built around. findings.title: Statcheck no nhst (Statistical Analysis and Results sections)
findings.description: A true zero, not a tool failure: the paper reports no t, F, chi-squared or r statistics anywhere in prose. findings.title: Data availability code withheld (Supplement 2, Data Sharing Statement)
findings.description: A mild instance that should not be overstated. Unlike the classic state-but-withhold pattern, the data here really are downloadable by anyone and the paper says exactly where. What is withheld is the derivation: the NSDUH recodes, the survey-design specification and the multinomial model syntax, without which a reader cannot reproduce the AORs even though they can obtain the raw data. Given that the analysis rests on correctly specifying PROC SURVEY strata, clusters and weights, that syntax is load-bearing. Also noted without weight: 'publically' is misspelled twice in this one-page statement.

findings.title: No preregistration (Statistical Analysis section and article metadata)
findings.description: Ordinary for a secondary analysis of a public survey and not a defect in itself. I record it because it is what decides how the two multiplicity findings should be read. With no preregistration, nothing distinguishes the covariate set, the four-level disability coding, the choice to stratify contrasts within each limitation level, or the ideation subgroup from analytic choices made after seeing the data. That places the reported comparison count as a FLOOR on the true multiplicity, which is the assumption those findings already state.
findings.location: Statistical Analysis section and article metadata
